notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0128b.stoa016.opp-l: Line 5: the clause rendered 'in the presence of the divinity they are always seen as present' reads garbled in the scan ('nec præterita trusirunt, Sed in presentia divinitatispræsenti semperducecermintur'); taken as 'transierunt ... praesentia semper cernuntur', so the rendering is uncertain. The final sentence of chapter 5 is syntactically loose in the Latin ('est ... et presciri, et facere, et eligere'); '[it belongs to him]' supplies the implied construction. Line 4: the scripture reference printed as Rom. VIII, 50 is taken as Rom. 8:30. Line 2: the edition marks this chapter 'III' though the next is also headed IV in the source numbering; the scan's 'IU' is read as III.

Ch. VIII: 'in istis gratis nulla justitia muneratur' is awkward; the sense seems to be that in the Israelites no righteousness is rewarded, the gift being free. Ch. VI: 'non Deo, sed ipsis relegentibus et credentibus profutura' read for 'prolutura'. Psalm numbers follow the Vulgate as given.

Ch. 10: 'Quod nullis humanis meritis reddit' read as 'reddi' (passive), parallel to 'donari'. 'misericors quero' read as 'misericors fuero', as repeated later. Ch. 11: 'inisse servatum' read as 'mansisse servatum'; 'mora- tione' as 'oratione'; 'Psal. CXXVIII, 34' should be Ps. 118:34. Psalm numbering follows the Vulgate as cited.

Many scanning errors silently corrected (e.g. 'lateris' read as 'fateris', 'conleitinens' as 'contemnens', 'ruIstis' as 'nostra', 'metuit' as 'meruit', 'munitícentia' as 'munificentia'). Ch. XIII: the sentence 'non solum vel natos in Adam ... sed lex ipsa peccati ... nisi etiam renatos' is garbled in the edition; rendered by sense. 'per singulos' (perhaps 'per singulos dies', 'daily') is uncertain. Ch. XVI: 'non dignatur angustias' is odd and may be corrupt (perhaps for 'non capitur angustiis'). Scripture references corrected where the printed numbers are misread: Ps. 118:37, Phil. 2:13, Ps. 102:8, 10, 2 Cor. 2:15-16, Deut. 10:14-16.

nodes.text: CHAPTER ONE. When in the sacred volumes of Scripture, whether in those that announce future things in the prophetic spirit, or in those that narrate past things with historical truth, or in those that hand down admonitions for life with apostolic authority, some passages seem to sound a different meaning, so that the reader is perplexed or the hearer troubled, it must be held, as known by sure and unshaken faith, that the mysteries of one and the same Spirit, apart from whom there is no truth at all, sound more openly in one place and a little more hiddenly in another. And so, if anything is held in suspense by a hidden meaning, or indicated briefly by the writer and set out less fully than the dullness of the human heart required, the reader should know that the truth appears more clearly here and lies more deeply hidden there, but is nowhere absent. And if, because of the greatness of the matter under inquiry, understanding does not readily come to the mind of the inquirer, especially if two statements of canonical authority seem to say different things about the unchangeable will of almighty God, then all these things must be directed to the rule of piety, so that it is held by unshaken definition that God is neither unjust, nor one who relaxes the merits of each person by some confused favouritism toward persons, nor weak, as though he were unable to carry out whatever he willed.

CHAPTER II. Under the yoke of this definition, then, so that our necks, wrongly free, may not run riot into sacrilegious rashness, let us speak, as far as we can by God's gift, of the hidden points of this question, which the blessed apostle Paul sets before diligent searchers in various places in words that differ not a little, and through which the Truth itself speaks to them. For, concluding a statement on the precedence of God's grace, worked out in a very broad and very powerful argument, he says: Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens (Rom. 9:18); while in another Epistle he himself speaks thus of the divine benevolence: Who wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4). For the question arises why some of them perish, when almighty God wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth; then again why he hardens some, having had mercy on others; or how he wills all men to be saved, when he himself hardens some so that they are not saved. As far as human justice goes, this seems unjust. But who would be so foolish, or rather who would so blaspheme, as to say that the justice of God must be argued about by the law of human justice? For that justice, if it is opposed to the justice of God, is surely unjust. For it is clear that from him who is supremely just flows everything that is in any way just. Who then will there be who would make the wisdom of God, which abides unchangeably and creates, rules and preserves all things that are, depend on the judgement of human wisdom? Of which the same apostle says that the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God (Rom. 8:7). And elsewhere: The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God (1 Cor. 3:19). Therefore the majesty of divine wisdom is not to be argued about by the judgement of human vanity.

CHAPTER III. But if anyone, by so nourishing his sins, is deceived by an image or shadow, or by the flattering conceit of pride, so as to say what the blessed apostle Paul saw at once that some would say (for he added: Someone will say: If he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens, why does he still find fault? For who resists his will? (Rom. 9:19)), let him know that by this statement we are rather compelled and constrained to humility and piety. For when that most eminent teacher, referring everything to God, denies it to human strength, what else is he urging but that we should hang upon God with our whole heart and ask from him the aids of salvation? Whoever, then, is troubled by this diversity in the dispensing of divine grace, and thinks it unjust that one should be denied what another has received, let him understand how divinely the Psalmist said: All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. 24:10); and let him recognise that God governs human affairs with such judgement that he either justly exacts the penalties owed or mercifully remits them. For the stain of the corrupted root has been so spread by transmission of the stock through the branches of the generations that not even an infant of one day is free from the guilt of the first transgression (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint), unless he has been set free by the unowed grace of the Saviour. And if not even this one is without sin, who could not have any of his own, it follows that he has contracted that other sin of which the Apostle says: Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and so it passed through to all men, in whom all sinned (Rom. 5:12). Whoever denies this surely denies that we are mortal in the first place. For if, as the Apostle says, through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, death could not enter except as sin entered. And since death is not a condition of nature but the penalty of sin, penalty must necessarily follow sin. But since death has passed through to all men, sin must necessarily have passed through to all. How original sin is born with little children we cannot see with the eyes of the flesh. But since we see that all born of Adam according to the flesh, even those who have already been reborn in Christ, are bound by the law of death, from the fact that we see little children dying at all times we are compelled to confess that little children are always born with original sin. For it could more easily happen that, though sin passed on, no penalty followed, than that someone who has no share in guilt should, with no communication of sin, take a share of the penalty. If then, as has been shown, we are all born debtors from the seed of the transgressor, since in him, as the Apostle says, all sinned, and the very lump from which we descend was condemned already at the beginning, let no one dare complain of his hardness, no one of his punishment, which is owed by the mere condition of birth even where there are no personal sins. But that God bestows unowed mercy on others, converted by a free calling, must by the reasoning of truth be referred not to the justice of distribution but to the most merciful bounty (another reading: liberty) of the giver. Will a debtor dare to accuse his creditor of injustice if, while remitting [a debt] to another, he has exacted from him what he owed? If then, in human contracts, there is no ground here for a plea by which the debtor might say that payment is unjustly exacted from him because he knows that the same creditor remitted to another debtor what he owed, who would burst out into such madness of profane speech as to accuse God of injustice if he gives unowed grace to one and pays back the owed penalty to another?

CHAPTER IV. And so, regarding the first part of this statement, which says: He has mercy on whom he wills, I think no one would dare dispute it except one unworthy of mercy. But at what follows, Whom he wills he hardens, the attention of the human mind is somewhat confused by the strangeness of the word. But it is not to be understood as though God produced in a man a hardness of heart that was not there. For what else is hardness but opposing the commandments of God? Hence the blessed Stephen said to the people: Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit (Acts 7:51). Whoever thinks this hardness is caused by God, because it is said, Whom he wills he hardens, let him look at the very beginning of the transgression, and consider that God gave a commandment, through which [man] produced in his heart the guilt of transgression, although he could not have been compelled even by the tempter himself had he refused consent. Therefore whatever punishment man, born as a result of that transgression, suffers, let him confess that it is justly and deservedly repaid. For God is said to harden the one whom he has not willed to soften. So too he is said to blind the one whom he has not willed to enlighten. So too to reject the one whom he has not willed to call. For those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he justified (Rom. 8:30). For he himself gave us to be, and he himself to be able to be good.

CHAPTER V. For his divinity foreknew us, his wisdom created us, his justice condemned us, his grace set us free. For though the world began in time from when it was made, in that light of divine foreknowledge, as something to be made, it could have no beginning; and all the men who have been born from Adam to the present day, or who will be born through the propagation of generations after our age, have already been born with God, and have passed through the course of their whole life, while nonetheless remaining in that light of the divine gaze. For God, who is neither enclosed by place nor preceded by time, is full of both the memory of all things past and the knowledge of all things to come; he neither turns back to the past in remembering, nor stretches forward to the future in hoping. And so it is with all things whatsoever that are moved by the motions of time, from that beginning in which was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word (John 1:1), to the end of all ages. Of which end the blessed Moses said: Lord, who reign for ever and ever (Exod. 15:18); and still future things are not hoped for, nor have past things passed away, but in the presence of the divinity they are always seen as present. By him, then, who is eternal and foreknowing, who is both just and merciful, who exercises owed severity and shows unowed mercy, and who has power in creating and choosing men as the potter has over the clay, some vessels were made for honour and others for dishonour. Before he made us, he foreknew us, and in that very foreknowledge, when he had not yet made us, he chose us. But by whom could this be done, except by him who calls the things that are not as though they were (Rom. 4:17)? For the Apostle says: Who chose us before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1:4). We were made within the world, and we were chosen before the world; and so in one and the same time, neither passing nor future, but continuous, or in whatever other way it can be expressed, if indeed there is time with God, [it belongs to him] both to foreknow, and to make, and to choose, and, his foreknowledge remaining unchangeably, to choose those who were to be made, whom he was going to make to be chosen. Let these things, as far as the rule of faith is concerned, be said beforehand with God's enlightenment.

CHAPTER VI. But now I see what slanderous perversity could object even from this. For it follows, [it says,] that if those whom he predestined he also called, and if those whom he called he also justified (Rom. 8:30), then those who were neither predestined nor called, and for this reason not justified either, ought to be innocent of all guilt, and punishments would unjustly be demanded of them on that day of recognition for the perversity of the life they have led. Let the apostle Paul say to these people: Is there injustice with God (Rom. 9:14)? Let him at once answer himself: By no means. And when this has been founded in a man's mind by sound piety, that there is no injustice with God, let him understand: He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens (ibid. 18), as if he were saying: On whom he wills he has mercy, and on whom he does not will he does not have mercy. And again let him understand this same thing as if it were said: To whom he wills he gives, and from whom he wills he demands what is owed. Whoever persists in calling this unjust, let him hear from the Apostle: O man, who are you to answer back to God (ibid. 20)? Fittingly indeed does apostolic authority rebuke impiety of this kind, striking home such weight by the heightening of the names when it says: O man, who are you to answer back to God? Man to God, clay to potter! For the same apostle added: Does the thing formed say to him who formed it: Why have you made me thus? Or does the potter not have power over the clay to make from the same lump one vessel for honour and another for dishonour (ibid. 21)? If then he has, or rather because the potter has power over the clay to make from the same lump one [vessel] for honour and another for dishonour, O man, who are you to answer back to God, because he has mercy on whom he wills and whom he wills he hardens? But before the blessed Apostle arrived at a conclusion of this kind in the course of his argument, he took above all this example from the ancient writings, in which to teach the hardening that is said to be done by God: The Scripture, he says, says to Pharaoh: For this very purpose I have raised you up, to show my power in you, and that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth (ibid. 17; Exod. 9:16). And in the same Scripture God is said most plainly to have hardened his heart, when he was speaking to Moses about the signs that were to be done through him against the Egyptians. For thus he says: But I will harden Pharaoh's heart, so that he will not let the people go (Exod. 4:21). From here the cunning slanderer, now flaunting himself openly, would weigh the justice of God by his own judgement, and answer with all the clamour he can: If he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills, why does he still find fault? For who resists his will? To his arrogance let the Apostle say: O man, who are you to answer back to God (Rom. 9:19-20)? But whoever, seeking piously, desires to find something, let him read again that place of the same Scripture where [God] first appeared to Moses in the fire of the bush, and so set his heart ablaze with the ardour of divine love that he spoke his testimonies before kings without being put to shame, as David says (Ps. 118:46); and there he will find that all this which [Scripture] puts forward, that God hardened Pharaoh's heart, pertains not to God's working but to his foreknowledge. For the Lord, speaking from the bush, says thus: But I know that Pharaoh king of Egypt will not let you go except by a mighty hand. But stretching out my hand I will strike the Egyptians with all the wonders that I shall do, and afterwards Pharaoh king of Egypt will let you go (Exod. 3:19-20). This is God's first utterance, by which he indicates Pharaoh's future will, just as he had foreseen it. Afterwards, amid the very showers of miracles, he is read to have said: But I will harden Pharaoh's heart, so that he will not let the people go (Exod. 4:21). Here it is now plainly understood that he repeated the first statement. For what is 'I will harden the heart' but 'I will not soften [it]'? For it is evident that, with justice remaining upon some and grace flowing out upon others, the statement of that Scripture was fulfilled, since God said to Pharaoh: For this very purpose I have raised you up, to show my power in you, and that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth (Exod. 9:16). For since God makes good use even of evil things, by the hardening of Pharaoh, by the scourges of Egypt, and by so many and such great miracles performed alike and in heaps among that nation, what else was accomplished but that the power of God, great with himself and full in himself, came to the knowledge of the human race, to be of profit not to God but to those who read and believe? That Pharaoh was not to be changed, nor all that nation which, after so many blows, tried to pursue with arms and war the people of God barely rescued from it, God foreknew in that lofty light of his providence. But he willed the destruction of those who were to perish to be a proof of salvation for the vessels of mercy predestined by him, and he used the perdition of some for the salvation of others, because the potter has power over the clay to make from the same lump one vessel for honour and another for dishonour (Rom. 9:21).

CHAPTER VII. This judgement of divine power in the election of men the blessed Apostle, mentioning it a little earlier, demonstrated by the most powerful examples, when he spoke of Rebecca's offspring while still in the womb, referring everything to the grace of God. For thus he says: And also Rebecca, having [conceived] by one act of intercourse with Isaac our father, when [the children] had not yet been born nor done anything good or evil, so that God's purpose according to election might stand, not from works but from him who calls, it was said that the elder shall serve the younger, as it is written: Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated; and at once he added: What shall we say? Is there injustice with God (Rom. 9:10-13; Gen. 25:23; Mal. 1:2)? And denying it he answered: By no means; so that the rest that follows should be referred back, held in suspense, to this statement by which he denied that there is injustice with God, and once referred be resolved [by it]. But what the aim of this apostolic argument achieved here is quite clear enough. For he compared not only brothers, but twins; and not only twins, but [twins] poured into the womb from a single act of intercourse: so that, since in those not yet born and not yet having done anything there could be no weight of merits, no obstacle against grace should be left even from the merits of the parents, which could vary at different times. Those merits of the parents, certainly, even if we grant that they either turned away or won divine protection for little children, whether good or bad, must have been equal in regard to twin offspring conceived in the same act of intercourse and brought forth into the light at the same moment. But if it is said that the divine judgement distinguished them by their future conduct, then surely what the Apostle stated beforehand will be made void when he says: Not from works but from him who calls it was said that the elder shall serve the younger. For he did not say 'from past works', but since he said generally 'not from works', he meant both past and future to be understood there: past, namely, which were none, future, which did not yet exist. Jacob was predestined a vessel for honour, because not from works but from him who calls it was said: The elder shall serve the younger.

CHAPTER VIII. And lest perhaps the vessels predestined for honour, by attributing something to their own strength, should deny the grace of the Creator, the Apostle in another place named them vessels of mercy, so that they might know that the whole of whatever they were they are according to mercy. For so the same Apostle says elsewhere too: And this is not from yourselves, but is the gift of God (Eph. 2:8). The blessed Moses also says to the people in Deuteronomy: And do not say in your heart: My strength and the might of my hand have made this great power for me; but you shall remember the Lord your God, because he himself gives you strength to do mighty deeds, that he may establish his covenant which he swore to your fathers (Deut. 8:17 ff.). Likewise a little later in the same place [he says] to them: Do not say in your heart, he says, when the Lord your God has consumed these nations before your face: Because of my righteousness the Lord has brought me in to inherit this good land. Not because of your righteousness, nor because of the holiness of your heart do you go in to inherit their land, but because of the iniquity of these nations the Lord will destroy them from before your face (Deut. 9:4-5). See how the onrush of a new presumption tries to overturn so ancient a doctrine of the Holy Spirit, proclaimed not only in the apostolic writings but also in the prophetic ones, and confirmed by the voice of the Holy Spirit at the very beginnings of the people of Israel. Clearly indeed, in one and the same place of Scripture, the blessed prophet shows the goodness and the severity of God, saying that the inheritance of that land is not rendered on account of the people's righteousness but given only by the grace of one who has mercy, while those others are driven out on account of their unrighteousness. See: in those, iniquity is justly punished; in these, no righteousness is freely rewarded. Nor was it enough for blessed Moses to have said that the inheritance of the land was granted to the people of Israel not on account of their own merits, unless he also added what he joined to it, by which to show them unworthy of every good. For there follows, after what we recalled above: And you shall know today that it is not because of your righteousness that the Lord your God gives you this good land to inherit, for you are a stiff-necked people (ibid. 6). Who would say here that a reward was rendered as owed for preceding merits? Who would not confess unowed grace? How often does the prophet say: They tempted him in the desert (Ps. 94:9)? How often did they deserve the anger of God by the turning away of their heart, and he saved them for his mercy's sake, that he might make his power known (Ps. 105:8)? This again the Apostle says: He endured with much patience the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, that he might show his riches upon the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory (Rom. 9:22-23).

Chapter 9. But lest, on the other hand, man, slackened into the lowest dregs of idleness, should believe that the steep path of virtue, which even with the help of God's grace can be walked only with toil, could be brought to him while he stays inert, and should apply the diligence of no labour to the pursuit of his own progress, God so ordered things, distributing times and duties between himself and man, that by his calling we should receive the beginnings of good things, and that, once called and enlightened, we should come to know the ways of his commandments by the understanding of a good mind, and should either choose or abandon them by free choice. Yet if, supported by his help, we followed them with continual devotion, at the end he would in turn crown in us an obedience that did not resist his commandments but was subject to them. But the free choice which we have from him flows with a downward slide toward wickedness, and while it can do nothing toward the nature of virtue when God's help forsakes it, for every kind of sin it stands supported by sufficient strength. For the law of sin born in the members draws [us], and God, according to his justice, will abandon those who withdraw from the light yoke of his commandments and the light burden, and who slide down into the harshest slavery of sin by a choice of the will free from righteousness. But those who have received the gift of calling with fitting devotion, who are not subjugated to fleshly allurements, who have been free of the vice of boasting, the torches of avarice, the wind of pride, and who, as far as lies in man, keeping God's good gifts in themselves, have brought all their zeal to spiritual exercises: these he both helps as they contend in the struggle of this life, and he bestows eternal crowns on the victors; and he in turn forsakes those who offend, hardens those who resist, condemns those who despise [him].

Chapter 10. Concerning the distribution of these stages, by which God either works in us or commands us to work something, let us question him from whose words arose the question which, if the Lord be present, we are trying to unravel, so that, his meanings being set out through various books in varied language but with one and the same intention, if anything lies hidden in this place, it may be opened up by comparison with another statement. That the apostle Paul was called by God we read either in that book where his deeds are narrated with all truth, or he himself confesses it in his Epistle, saying: Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, called [to be] an apostle (Rom. 1:1). And in the second place, having followed the calling and done all that was in a man, he himself speaks thus: I laboured more than all of them (1 Cor. 15:10). But not attributing even this to himself, he added with anxious devotion: Yet not I, but the grace of God with me (ibid.). So for one who had been called and had followed the calling through works of righteousness, what else remained but that, freed from the body of this death, he should come to the blessedness of that other life which has been promised to all the saints by the mouth of Truth? That this is not rendered to any human merits but is given by the bounty of the grace of God the giver, he answers himself, after the groans with which he had said: Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God, he says, through Jesus Christ our Lord (Rom. 7:24-25). This distribution, then, by which we said that men are called by God when no merits exist, and that, once called, they need God's supports in order to do anything good, the Apostle shows by an example taken from the ancient writings: after he had referred that election concerning the two twins, rejecting all praise of merits, to God's grace and judgement, seeing what impious chatter might blaspheme, he said: Is there injustice with God (Rom. 9:14)? And he goes on: By no means. And as if it were said to him, 'How do you prove it?', he thought the authority of his own teaching of little weight unless he also taught his view by an example from the law. For he wished what Moses had said to be understood thus: I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I have been merciful (Exod. 33:19): so that we should believe that the first mercy is granted beforehand to men in the calling, which alone is not sufficient for living rightly if he who called forsakes [them]. And therefore it was added: And I will show mercy to whom I have been merciful, so that it may be plain that from God are received even the very works of mercy by which, when we seem to bestow them, we merit the mercy of God. For so he says in the Gospel: Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them (Matt. 5:7). Had the Apostle not understood it so, he would never have taken care to insert this testimony into his argument on behalf of the good things of grace.

Chapter 11. But if anyone is troubled that not all, even of those who have already been called, merit to attain the second grace, that is, the gift of living rightly, as the Lord says in the Gospel, Many are called, but few chosen (Matt. 20:16): let him understand from this what sort of thing he is striving to defend against the grace of God who flatters himself about free choice. For whoever, having abandoned the gift of the divine calling, have flowed back into impious faithlessness, for them, since they forsake the grace of God, choice suffices to fulfil what they wished. For see how the Psalmist, with the truth of the prophetic spirit, sings the order of God's mercies which the Apostle interprets from the meaning of Moses: Hear, he says, my people, and I will testify to you (Ps. 80:9). What did he want them to hear, which he was speaking with testimony? What, surely, but the commandments of life? As another prophet says: Hear, Israel, the commandments of life (Bar. 3:9). But what these commandments of life are the Psalmist adds, and goes on: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt (Ps. 80:11). And that these are the commandments of life the Lord showed in the prayer with which he commended his disciples to the Father, saying: For this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). After this calling there follows that which he both wills to belong to the efforts of men and shows cannot be completed without him: for this is what the Apostle says: For from him we have to will and to accomplish according to [his] good will (Phil. 2:13). From him we have to will, because he calls and enlightens; from him to accomplish, since it belongs to us to strive for the good things which he also granted us to will. And not carelessly did the Apostle, when he had said that from him we have both to will and to accomplish, add 'according to good will', so that they may see again and again where they have, from God's justice, the free choice they boast of. But let us see, also in the continued discourse of this psalm, that order in which the Lord distributes various mercies by the dispensation of times, as the Apostle understood Moses to have said. For what does he say after he had taught those called, saying: For I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt? Open wide your mouth, he says, and I will fill it (Ps. 80:11). Here again something appears to have been reserved to man, which he ought to do through free choice. For he is commanded to open wide his mouth, but God promises that he will fill it. As he had also said to his disciples in the Gospel: Do not think how or what you are to speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you (Matt. 10:19-20). This alone he referred to them, that they should willingly undertake every constraint of tribulation for the truth, but the accomplishment he promised [to keep] in his own hands. What place, then, is reserved to free choice, so that human nature, though supported by rational dignity, is not sufficient by itself to fulfil what it wishes without God's help, the Psalmist at once shows: And my people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not attend to me (Ps. 80:12). He who had said when he called, Hear, my people, and I will speak; Israel, and I will testify to you: what had he, testifying, commended to the minds of his hearers? I am the Lord your God. And what had he commanded to be done by them, whom, freed from the land of Egypt and the darkness of ignorance, he had led out into the light of his commandments by the splendour of calling? Open wide your mouth, he says. And at once, as if he were saying, 'If you wish to open it while I forsake you, it will profit nothing', he so added: and I will fill it. What then does he who had called, and had taught those called, add about them in a complaining voice? And my people, he says, did not hear my voice, and Israel did not attend to me. Let the defender of free choice against God come forth now; let him hear the Apostle saying, when he spoke of his good labours: Yet not I, but the grace of God with me (1 Cor. 15:10). Let him hear the voice of God in the psalm saying of those whom he had forsaken: And I let them go according to the desires of their heart; they will walk in their own wills (Ps. 80:13). Let him hear one and the same Apostle, concerning the various periods of his life, attributing only evils to himself, but all good things to the grace of God: I who was formerly a blasphemer, he says, and a persecutor (1 Tim. 1:13). And in another place: By the grace of God I am what I am (1 Cor. 15:10). When he said, I who was formerly a blasphemer and a persecutor, no mention of grace was joined to the wicked deed, because, as has been said, the nature of human freedom is sufficient to itself for wickedness. But when he spoke of the blessedness of his present life, he said: By the grace of God I am what I am. And that order in which God has mercy by calling, and then has mercy by helping in efforts begun, as has been narrated and set out in the sequence of the psalm, blessed Paul the apostle also kept in a continuous narration. For if the excerpted testimonies are read over in the order in which he placed them, he speaks thus: By the grace of God, he says, I am what I am. This is the first mercy, which the works of free will follow. But that good works might follow the calling of the apostle Paul, what does he say? And his grace in me was not in vain. For what did you do? I laboured, he says, more than all. Do not be too proud, O defender of free choice, hearing Paul boast of his labours; attend to what follows: Yet not I, but the grace of God with me. I think indeed that none of those who blaspheme against the grace of God with a heart exalted before ruin, as it is written (Prov. 16:18), will assume so much shameless arrogance as to think himself either equal to the merits of the blessed prophet David or even to be preferred to them. Leaving aside for the moment that first reward of his, which no one would fail to confess as unowed, namely the kingdom conferred [on him], let us weigh the intentions and feelings of his prayers and confessions. He himself indeed declares in the psalm: Blessed is the man whom you instruct, Lord, and teach from your law (Ps. 93:12). But let us see whether for him, already instructed and sufficiently taught all knowledge of the law according to Jewish instruction, this alone sufficed for blessedness. Why then did the same man cry again to the Lord: Give me understanding, and I will search your law, and I will keep it with my whole heart (Ps. 118:34)? It was little that he had asked for understanding to search the law, unless he also indicated that help was necessary to keep it, saying: And I will keep it with my whole heart; as if he said: Then I will keep it with my whole heart, if you give understanding.

CHAPTER XII. Let that proud defender of his own will still reply to this that the prophet asked for the aid of divine help only for understanding the divine commandments, which he would nevertheless have fulfilled by his own strength. If this is so, I wish to search out a little from you, blessed David, the hidden things of your thoughts. Where then, I ask you, does the battle of flesh and spirit come from? Where does the apostolic struggle come from, as you yourself confess? Even when you are certainly enlightened and instructed by the gift of understanding which you had asked of God, you cry out and say: Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity (Ps. 118:37). For if you have received, as you asked, understanding to distinguish vanity from truth, why do you not turn your eyes away from the vanity that displeases you? If you rebuke avarice, why do you not separate yourself from it by your own choice and incline your heart to the commandments of salvation, but cry to God as one weak in all things: Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to avarice, unless because the law of sin born in the members prompts avarice, and the holy man still wants to turn away his eyes and cannot do it by himself? And so the flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. 5:17): and from this strife nothing frees [us] except grace, which is given to small and great through our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom. 7:25). For to will is present with me, but to accomplish I do not find (Rom. 7:18). Yet even the willing itself is not from us but is the gift of God, since from him we have both to will and to accomplish, according to good will (Phil. 2:13). Blessed therefore are you, since you agree with the apostles of Christ in equality both of teaching and of battle: for in your writings we recognize the wars of the apostles, and we find your struggles in the apostolic letters.

CHAPTER XIII. Where does this diversity of things and wills come from in one and the same man, who consists of soul and body, unless because man, despising the just judgements of God, man [despising] God, the creature the Creator, the lowest the highest, finds within himself the penalties of disobedience and the defiance of the inferior part? For by what justice should a creature serve a creature, though the worse the better, if it itself refused to serve the Creator, whatever sort of creature it is? But not even this suffices for the penalty, that the worse part should fight against the better affections of the heart, unless it also very often overcame, led into captivity and possessed [it]; and unless the law of sin not only claimed for the service of its motions men born in Adam, but also assailed, while its prompting remains, those reborn in Christ. For truly through that gift of regeneration the guilt has been remitted, [but] the condition has not been dissolved; it is grace that blots out the bonds of old debts, not yet separating from fleshly passion the man still living in the flesh, so that in time to come every man may implore divine help at each [moment]. And since the law could not so much take away sin as show it, the sin which claimed for itself men everywhere as they were born, and plunged those possessed by consent to concupiscence into eternal destruction, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the Word of the Father, equal and coeternal with the Father, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7); and though he himself was not sin, he was made sin by the flesh he assumed, so that, man being healed from the sin of the flesh, he might condemn sin in the flesh. He came to seek what had perished (Luke 19:10), to heal what was sick, to raise what lay fallen, having power to forgive sins, to give what he did not owe, to remit what was owed to him, and, all stains of the old guilt being blotted out, to restore the nature he had made. From among those for whom just severity had decreed punishment, according to the ineffable mercy of his hidden disposition, he chose vessels which he would make for honour; and some he released from the wrath to come by the gift of a free calling, others he left and reserved for the judgement of equity, yet he did not take away from them the capacity to recognize the truth. And so the fullness of divine foreknowledge was fulfilled, justice flowing upon some, grace streaming forth upon others; so that, those perishing whom God had foreknown would perish, and those being saved whom in that secret election he had foreknown were to be saved, the Church, spread through the whole world, might be multiplied.

CHAPTER XIV. Rejoice therefore, whoever you are who have been enlightened, and acknowledge the grace you did not merit. Groan, whoever you are who have been hardened, and confess the justice. Say, whoever you are who rejoice that you have been washed from the original contagion by the bath of grace: The Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and of great mercy. He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities (Ps. 102:8, 10). Say, whoever you are who are condemned: You are just, Lord, in all that you have done to us, and all your judgements are true: for in truth and judgement you have brought all these things upon us because of our sins (Dan. 3:27-28); and do not ascribe the blame for your hardening to injustice in God, since all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. 24:10), so that neither those who have obtained mercy from God may glory in anything of their own merits by the judgement of truth, nor those who have been hardened and condemned may believe they can have an excuse for their guilt from this, that they did not obtain any mercy by which they might be converted. This mercy, then, Pharaoh did not receive, and therefore his free choice sufficed him for perishing; and no one will be so ignorant of the divine Scriptures as to dare to say that he suffered all those things unjustly. Or perhaps, if we think piously of God as is fitting, do we find that mercy was given even to Pharaoh? For the patience of God ought to have availed him for salvation, by which, deferring the just and deserved punishment, he thickened the frequent blows of miracles. Could he not, just as, struck by the scourges, he drove out the people, so also, believing the miracles, have acknowledged a God of such great power? If it is said that Pharaoh could not have been changed because God had foreknown that he would not be changed, the reply is that God's foreknowledge does not compel a man to be such as God foreknew; rather it foreknows that he will be such as he is going to be, although God did not make him so. If he compelled him to be so, he would certainly be compelling what is not. Further, if he had foreknown that what is not would be, it is not foreknowledge; and how impiously that is said of God, anyone may observe who flatters himself in his sins on the ground that God foreknew he would be a sinner.

CHAPTER XV. Nevertheless I think there may perhaps be someone who says that the way is less fit for salvation if someone is scourged without being stirred by any inward calling. How then did Nebuchadnezzar merit fruitful repentance (Dan. 4:33)? Did he not repent after countless impieties when he was scourged, and receive again the kingdom he had lost? But Pharaoh (Exod. 8 ff.) was made harder by the very scourges, and perished. Here let him who, being too high-minded in his heart, passes judgement on the divine counsel give me a reason why the medicine prepared by one physician availed for one man to destruction, for another to salvation, unless because the good odour of Christ is to some the odour of life unto life, to others the odour of death unto death (2 Cor. 2:15-16)? As to nature, both were men; as to rank, both kings; as to circumstance, both held possession of the captive people of God; as to punishment, both were mercifully warned by scourges. What then made their ends different, except that one, feeling the hand of God, groaned at the remembrance of his own iniquity, while the other fought with his free choice against God's most merciful truth? Here whoever answers that divine aid was present to the one that he might be changed, and absent from the other so that he was hardened, and contends that this is unjust, on account of which the Apostle, setting the ends of things themselves in the will of God, said, He has mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardens (Rom. 9:18), while the Lord says, Without me you can do nothing (John 15:5), let him understand that all those things are either accomplished with the Lord's help or permitted by his forsaking, so that he may nevertheless know that nothing at all is permitted against the Lord's will.

CHAPTER XVI. But we return to the little children, we return to the twins; it is too little what I have said: we return to those not yet born, who were both conceived in the same intercourse and were to be brought forth into the light at the same moment. The judgement of the divine will appearing different and divergent for them, the magnitude of the question confounds the minds of men who dispute too proudly about the will of God. Raise your voice now with all your strength, you unjust accuser of the just one, and tell me what evil the one committed, what good the other merited. And it is not I who answer you, but Paul the apostle: Neither of them, indeed, merited anything; but the potter has power over the clay to make from the same lump one vessel for honour, another for dishonour (Rom. 9:21). You will say: Why? What is this so confused diversity of judgement? Again let him refute this presumption and say: O man, who are you to answer back to God (ibid. 9:20)? Especially since our attention, turned to that comparison with human acts, answers that a creditor cannot be accused of injustice who, with two debtors, has chosen to make such a judgement as to forgive one and exact from the other what is owed by both. And certainly it is plain that in all the acts and contracts of human dealings, this [capacity] by which we seem to discern something, to judge, to approve some justice, flows into the hearts of our lowliness from the ineffable fullness of divine justice, as blessed John confirms in his Gospel, since we have all received of his fullness (John 1:16). If this is so, with what impudence, pray, will man judge God, the clay the potter, not only saying, Why have you made me thus? but also prying into others with damnable curiosity and saying, Why from the same lump have you made one thus and another thus? If the human race, which, as is agreed, was first created from nothing, were not born with the due origin of death and sin, and yet the almighty Creator wished to condemn some of them to eternal destruction, who would say to the almighty Creator, Why have you done thus? For he who had granted them being when they were not had power over the end for which they should exist; nor could the rest say why the divine choice differed when the merits of all were equal, since the potter has power over the clay to make from the same lump one vessel for honour, another for dishonour (Rom. 9:21). But now, since a just penalty is rendered to the condemned, and unowed grace is given to the saved, who is so forgetful of the human condition as to investigate the secrets of the divine mind, so that, when he himself has deservedly incurred the penalty, he asks why another has received the grace which was not owed to him? That this divine election is not repaid to merits but given to men by the sole munificence of [God's] will, Moses showed even then, though he was teaching a carnal people. For he says plainly to the people in Deuteronomy: Behold, to the Lord your God belongs heaven, and the heaven of heaven, the earth and all that is in it; yet the Lord chose your fathers to love them, and chose their seed after them, you, above all nations. And he added: Be circumcised therefore from the hardness of your heart, and do not harden your neck any longer (Deut. 10:14-16). But that this hardness of heart remained in them, as we have already said above, blessed Stephen showed when he rebuked the Jews. For in the Acts of the Apostles, as he himself says: Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit (Acts 7:51). Where did the stiff neck come from in that people which was chosen out of the whole world, which merited to be freed from slavery by ten miracles, to which the law was given, for whose salvation the mouths of all the prophets served, from which Christ was made according to the flesh, and to whom he was sent, unless because blindness in part has happened to Israel until Israel, adopted out of the fullness of the Gentiles, should enter into the kingdom (Rom. 11:25); and the Lord has shut up all in unbelief, so that all should need the mercy of the Saviour? Touching on the sacraments of this divine counsel, and the mystery of majesty, which, although he knew them through the greatness of his revelations, he nevertheless succumbed to because of human weakness, even he who, despite his persecutions and blasphemies, merited to be named a Vessel of election cries out in wonder: O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God (ibid. 11:33)! confessing both that his ways are unsearchable and that the judgements of God are unsearchable. With him therefore, when such things are inquired into, let us wonder; and holding fast to the sentence that there is no iniquity with God, if there is anything in what is inquired into which exceeds the measure of our understanding and does not deign [to enter] the narrows of our intellect, let us confess that it abides with unshaken equity in that fullness of divine justice, mercy and foreknowledge. Lest, disputing about the higher secrets of the divine will otherwise than the measure of our condition allows, we abandon the justice of God and, desiring to establish our own, fall into the lowest abyss of defiance.
